slides.text:
A Go string never changes, so joining many pieces with `+` makes a new copy each time. `strings.Builder` collects the pieces in one buffer and hands over the string at the end.

In this module you will write into a builder, add bytes and characters, and use it inside loops and functions.

A builder is like an empty box you add text to. You write pieces in order, then read the whole text once.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
box = empty builder
add "a" to box
add "b" to box
text = read box
      -> "ab"

slides.text: Writing to a builder does not copy the text collected so far. That is why it beats `+=` when a loop adds many pieces.

exercises.title: Write into a builder
exercises.guide: Collect text in a builder, then take the result.

chunks.guide: A `strings.Builder` starts empty. Declare it with `var`, no setup needed.

notes.text: A buffer you add text to. Its empty value is ready to use.
Appends to the end, without copying what is there.

chunks.guide: `String` returns everything written so far. `Len` counts its bytes.

notes.text: Turns the collected text into a string.
The size in bytes, like len on a string.

exercises.title: Build in a loop
exercises.guide: Write one line per step, then print the whole text.

chunks.guide: Declare a builder and the steps to write.
Write each step and a line break. The builder keeps adding to the same buffer.
`Print` adds no line break of its own: the text already has them.

exercises.title: Fill the builder
exercises.guide: Declare a builder, write two pieces and print the text.

exercises.title: What is wrong with +=?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the reason a builder is better.
options: It does not compile inside a loop
A string cannot be changed with +=
Each += copies the whole text again
+= only joins two strings at a time
exercises.explanation: A string never changes, so every += builds a new one and copies all the old text. On a long loop that adds up. A builder appends to one buffer instead.

exercises.title: Bytes and runes
exercises.guide: Add a single byte and a single character.

chunks.guide: Start with two letters in the builder.

notes.text: Takes a byte. A quoted ASCII character fits.
Adds the character in its UTF-8 form.

chunks.guide: `Len` counts bytes, and é takes two of them.

slides.text: In real programs a builder usually lives inside a loop or a function: write the pieces, then return one string. It can also be emptied and reused, or told how much room to expect.

exercises.title: Separators between items
exercises.guide: Write a comma before every name except the first.

chunks.guide: Declare a builder and the names.
The index tells which name is first. Only later ones get a separator.

notes.text: Skips the separator before the first name.

exercises.title: A dash and a letter
exercises.guide: Add the dash as a byte and the accented letter as a character.

exercises.title: Builder inside a function
exercises.guide: Hide the builder in a function that returns the text.

chunks.guide: The package and imports are already in the file. The builder lives inside, and the caller only gets the finished string.

notes.text: The caller gets a plain string, not the builder.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: String returns the text as it is at that moment. Writing more later does not change a string that was already taken.

exercises.title: Reserve room and reuse
exercises.guide: Reserve space ahead, then empty the builder and start again.

chunks.guide: `Grow` reserves room when you know the size. The text stays empty.

notes.text: Only prepares space for 32 more bytes. Nothing is written.

chunks.guide: Write a draft and check its size.
`Reset` empties the builder so it can be used again.

notes.text: Throws away the text written so far.
